newsitem.title: UK: Hyder warns on level of windfall tax.
newsitem.headline: Hyder warns on level of windfall tax.

text.p: British multi-utility Hyder Plc warned on Monday that a one-off "windfall" tax proposed by the new Labour government should not be at a level which could threaten discretionary investment or voluntary price cuts.

"It should be at a level where we would not be obliged to re-examine our discretionary and environmental investments and voluntary customer discounts within the water and sewerage business," Hyder said in a statement with annual results.

The new Labour government, which swept to power in a landslide victory on May 1, has made a one-off tax on the "excess profits" of privatised utilities to fund a three billion pound plan to cut unemployment a central plank of its first budget, scheduled for July 2.
Hyder said it had signed up to the government's 10-point plan of action to tackle drought, proposed at a crisis summit in mid-May, and added that it was on course to meet leakage targets.
Hyder posted year pre-tax profits of 208.2 million pounds, up from 112.9 million pounds previously and paid out a dividend of 43.9 pence per share, up from 38.7 pence.

The company said it was "happy to see mandatory leakage targets provided these reflect the different circumstances of each company," adding it felt its existing targets "strike the right balance for the present."
Part of the government's 10-point plan called for the introduction of mandatory targets to cut leaks for companies, as nearly 800 million gallons of supply seeps out of pipes every day.
Hyder said it was "committed to maintaining unrestricted supplies to our customers in the future", adding that there had been no ban on using water in garden hoses in its area for seven years.

Britain is suffering its worst drought for 200 years and water companies have come under heavy criticism from the government and consumer lobbies for not cutting non-essential domestic use during the very hot summer of 1995.
